title: A telegram with a word limit
allegory: An autoencoder is like a sender and a receiver who may pass only a five-word telegram: to let the receiver redraw the picture, they invent a private shorthand that keeps only what matters.
map: the sender squeezing the picture into words
the encoder, mapping x to a small vector z
the word limit on the telegram
the bottleneck: z is much narrower than x
the receiver redrawing from the telegram
the decoder, mapping z back to x̂
scoring how different the redraw looks
a shorthand that only works for telegrams they actually sent
a latent space that is only trained where real inputs land

chapters.name: What is the gist?
chapters.note: most pixels are predictable from the rest

cap.1: A picture of a handwritten digit is hundreds of numbers, but most are predictable from the rest. What is the short version, and who decides?
cap.2: You want a compact code for each image with no labels saying what matters. The trick: make a network find the code by forcing it to rebuild the image from it.
cap.3: Unsupervised representation learning: no labels, just a reconstruction objective. Compression through a bottleneck forces the code to keep what best predicts the input.

cap.1: A sender may use only five words to describe a drawing, and a receiver must redraw it from them. Practise together and they invent a shorthand.
cap.2: Encoder: image to a small vector z. Decoder: z back to an image. Train both so the output matches the input. The narrow z is the telegram's word limit.
cap.3: x → encoder → z, with d_latent ≪ d_input, → decoder → x̂, trained end to end. The bottleneck rules out the identity map, so z must be a compressed code.

cap.1: The pair is scored only on how different the redraw is from the original. Nobody tells them what the words should mean.
cap.2: The loss is reconstruction error, for example mean squared error per pixel. Backprop runs through decoder and encoder together, so the code is learned, not designed.
cap.3: L = ‖x − D(E(x))‖². With linear E, D and squared error, the learned code spans the same subspace as the top principal components; nonlinear E, D learn a curved version.

cap.1: Wide, then narrow, then wide again. The middle is the telegram: too small to copy the picture, so it must keep only what matters.
cap.2: Encoder layers shrink, the code is smallest, decoder layers grow back to image size. Make the middle as wide as the input and the network can simply copy.
cap.3: If d_latent is large enough to pass x through losslessly, the identity is reachable and nothing is learned. The bottleneck, or another constraint, is what forces structure.

chapters.name: The messy map

right.title: a random point in code space

chapters.verdict: A good compressor is not a good generator. That gap is why VAEs exist.

cap.1: The shorthand only works for telegrams they actually sent. Make one up and the receiver draws nonsense. Similar telegrams can mean unrelated things.
cap.2: Nothing asks the encoder to use the code space sensibly, so a random z often decodes to junk and neighbouring codes can decode to unrelated digits. ARENA shows this with a latent grid.
cap.3: The objective only constrains z where real inputs land; the rest of latent space is unregularised, so you cannot sample from it. VAEs add a KL term to fix that (Kingma and Welling, 2014).

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: A compressed code the model invented itself
VAEs and GANs start from this shape
SAEs flip it: wider, not narrower, plus sparsity

cap.1: This shape returns in interpretability: sparse autoencoders rebuild a model's insides, but go wider instead of narrower and allow only a few active words.
cap.2: Sparse autoencoders reuse encode-then-rebuild on a model's activations. They swap the narrow bottleneck for a wide layer with a sparsity penalty, to find readable features.
cap.3: Encode, reconstruct, penalise: the SAE keeps this objective but trades the bottleneck for overcompleteness plus L1 sparsity, the course's tool for pulling features out of superposition.

readouts.label: picture rebuilt
readouts.f: Math.round(100 * sum(range(8).map(i => i < k ? pow(r, i) : 0)) / sum(range(8).map(i => pow(r, i)))) + '%'

caption.1: Each bar is one kind of detail the code keeps. Slide the width, then slide how fast detail fades: when it fades fast, three numbers rebuild nearly everything.
caption.2: Real data has a few big directions of variation and many small ones. A narrow code keeps the big ones. When detail does not fade (far right), every cut costs the same.
caption.3: For a linear AE with squared error, the best k-dim code spans the top-k variance directions and the error is the sum of the dropped variances. Nonlinear AEs bend this; same logic.

where_else: VAEs and GANs, which turn the decoder half into a generator
Sparse autoencoders on model activations: the same encode-and-rebuild, but wider and sparse
Transcoders: the same shape trained to rebuild an MLP's output from its input
Compression in general: a code is good if the receiver can rebuild the message from it

hamming.what: A network trained to rebuild its own input through a narrow middle layer, which forces that layer to become a compressed code.
hamming.when: When you want a compact representation without labels, or as the starting shape for VAEs and sparse autoencoders.
hamming.why: Rebuilding through a bottleneck means the code has to keep what matters most about the input and drop the rest.

object.title: The information hourglass
object.subtitle: Wide in, a narrow neck, wide out: everything the redraw needs has to squeeze through the neck.

cap.1: Wide in, narrow middle, wide out: an hourglass for information.
cap.2: Encoder, code, decoder. The tube is the path every image takes.
cap.3: E: x → z, D: z → x̂, with dim z ≪ dim x.

cap.1: The neck is a handful of numbers. Everything the redraw needs has to fit through here.
cap.2: The code z is the bottleneck. Its size is the telegram's word limit.
cap.3: The bottleneck caps the information z can carry, so the code keeps the highest-value directions of variation.

cap.1: Both halves are trained together, scored only on how well the redraw matches the original.
cap.2: One loss, reconstruction error, trains encoder and decoder end to end.
cap.3: Joint optimisation of E and D on ‖x − D(E(x))‖²; the code's meaning is whatever makes decoding easiest.

cap.1: Picture the neck as wide as the ends: the sand pours straight through and nothing is learned.
cap.2: No bottleneck means the network can learn to copy. The squeeze is what makes the code useful.
cap.3: Remove the constraint and the identity is optimal: zero loss, no structure. Some constraint is always required.

cap.1: Now imagine a bulge where the neck was: that is a sparse autoencoder, kept honest by using only a few words at once.
cap.2: SAEs make the middle wider than the input and add a sparsity penalty instead of a bottleneck.
cap.3: Overcomplete dictionary plus L1: sparsity, not width, supplies the constraint that forces structure.

predict.q: You make the code as wide as the input. What does the autoencoder learn?

options.t: Possibly nothing useful: it can just copy

predict.why: Without a bottleneck, or another constraint like sparsity, copying is allowed, so there is no pressure to find structure.

predict.q: You decode a random point from a plain autoencoder's code space. What do you usually get?

options.t: Often junk: that region was never trained

predict.why: Only the codes of real images were trained. VAEs regularise the whole space so random points decode sensibly.

predict.q: A sparse autoencoder's hidden layer is...

options.t: Wider than its input, with a sparsity penalty
Narrower than its input, like this one

predict.why: SAEs trade the bottleneck for sparsity: many possible words, only a few used at once.

object.where: Any encode, squeeze, decode pipeline: codecs, VAEs, and sparse autoencoders on model activations.
